court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A boarding house keeper sued to recover the value of trunks retained under a claimed lien for an unpaid board bill; the court held the boarding house keeper failed to prove the wife personally agreed to pay for the family's board and lodging, since such liability presumptively falls on the husband absent an express agreement by the wife.

quotes.text: A contract for board and lodging made by a married woman presumptively creates a liability against the husband; and the boarding house keeper, in order to bind the wife, has the burden of proving that she in express terms undertook to pay therefor.

Board and lodging are necessaries, and where the defendant had notice that the plaintiff had a husband she was bound to assume that she was contracting with him for the support of his family, unless the plaintiff undertook in express terms to assume the burden which the law casts upon the husband.
it would seem that the defendant had failed to establish any kind of liability on the part of the plaintiff.

notes: Core holding is about spousal liability for necessaries, but the court treats the boarding-house board-and-lodging contract as an ordinary, legitimate business arrangement throughout.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A hotel keeper's liquor tax certificate was properly revoked under the 1905 statute because his hotel's bedrooms were separated by partitions thinner than the three inches required for lodger accommodations, but the building superintendent could not lawfully destroy the partitions without a judgment or order of a competent judicial authority.

quotes.text: such hotel building contained at least ‘ten bedrooms, * * * each room properly furnished to accommodate lodgers and separated by partitions at least three inches thick extending from floor to ceiling.’
it certainly had no power to authorize an officer to destroy the plaintiff’s property without the judgment or order of a competent judicial authority.
that his building did ‘not comply with the laws, ordinances, and regulations in relation to hotels’

notes: Regulation of lodger-bedroom construction sustained (adverse), but summary destruction of the partitions without judicial process was enjoined (favorable) — marked mixed.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: A tenant who leased a house to operate the business of renting furnished rooms sold that business, together with the lease and its security deposit, by an unambiguous bill of sale; the court held she could not avoid the transfer of her interest in the security by claiming she could not read English, absent any showing of fraud or mistake.

quotes.text: The plaintiff occupied the house for carrying on the business of renting furnished rooms.
executed to her a bill of sale of said business, “together with the good will and lease with security thereon and also all the goods and chattels” described in an annexed schedule.

she could not, in the absence of any showing of fraud or imposition, avoid the effect of the bill of sale as a transfer of her right to the security by asserting that she could not read English and did not know that she was making such transfer.

notes: Case treats the furnished-rooms rental business, its lease, and its security deposit as ordinary transferable commercial assets; individual lodgers' occupancy duration not addressed, hence 'unclear'.
